title: Contra Academicos
author: Augustine

passages.original: — Quorum tandem? — Ille: Eorum scilicet, qui sapientes fuerunt. — Tum Licentius: Carneades, inquit, tibi sapiens non uidetur? — Ego, ait, Graecus non sum; nescio Carneades iste qui fuerit. — Quid, inquit Licentius, de illo nostro Cicerone quid tandem existimas ? — Hic cum diu tacuisset: Sapiens fuit, inquit. — Et ille: Ergo eius de hac re sententia habet apud te aliquid ponderis? — Habet, inquit. — Accipe igitur quae sit; nam eam tibi excidisse arbitror.
passages.english: "Whose, then?" He [said]: "Those, of course, who were wise." Then Licentius said: "Does Carneades not seem wise to you?" "I am not a Greek," he said; "I do not know who this Carneades of yours was." "Well then," said Licentius, "what, pray, do you think of our own Cicero?" After he had been silent for a long time, he said: "He was wise." And the other: "So his opinion on this matter carries some weight with you?" "It does," he said. "Then hear what it is, for I think it has slipped your mind."

passages.original: sed quoniam iam dudum disposita profectio interrumpere me conpellit, pro meo quoque munere geminatam sibi potestatem particeps mecum iudicii non rennuet usque in reditum meum; uideo enim hoc uestrum certamen longius progressurum. — Et cum discessit: Quid,inquit Licentius,temere concesseras? profer. — Et ille: Temere dedi, inquit, Ciceronem fuisse sapientem. — Ergone Cicero sapiens non fuit, a quo in latina lingua philosophia et incoata est et perfecta? — Etsi concedam, inquit, esse sapientem, non omnia tamen eius probo. — Atqui oportet multa eius alia refellas, ut non inpudenter hoc, de quo agitur, inprobare uidearis.
passages.english: "But since a journey arranged long ago compels me to break off, my partner in judging will not refuse the power doubled for him, my share included, until my return; for I see that this contest of yours will go on a good while longer." And when he had left, Licentius said: "What was it you had granted rashly? Out with it." And he said: "I granted rashly that Cicero was wise." "So Cicero was not wise, by whom philosophy in the Latin tongue was both begun and brought to completion?" "Even if I grant," he said, "that he is wise, still I do not approve everything of his." "But you must refute many other things of his, so that you do not seem shameless in rejecting this point at issue."

passages.original: Diu ille tacuit; deinde: En, inquit, iterum definio, si hoc tu numquam finire statuisti. sapientia est uia recta, quae ad ueritatem ducat. — Similiter et hoc, inquit ille, refellitur; nam cum apud Uergilium Aeneae dictum est a matre: perge modo et, qua te ducit uia, dirige gressum, sequens hancuiam ad id, quod dictumerat, id est ad uerum, peruenit. contende, si placet, ubi pedem ille incedens posuit. sapientiam posse dici; quamquam stulte prorsus istam descriptionem tuam conor effringere;
passages.english: He was silent for a long time; then he said: "Look, I define it again, since you have resolved never to put an end to this. Wisdom is the right way that leads to truth." "This too is refuted in the same way," said the other; "for when in Virgil Aeneas was told by his mother, 'Only go on, and where the way leads you, direct your step,' he, following this way, arrived at what had been said, that is, at the truth. Maintain, if you like, that the place where he set his foot as he walked can be called wisdom. And yet it is quite foolish of me to try to break down this description of yours;
passages.notes: The text 'contende... sapientiam posse dici' appears to be ironic: the point is that on this definition the road Aeneas walked would be 'wisdom'; punctuation in the edition is uncertain.

passages.original: atque ille statim non modo negotii genus sed etiam, in quo ille uehementer clamabat admirans, ipsum fundi nomen pronuntiauit, cum ita esset absurdum, ut uix eius Flaccianus ipse meminisset. iam illud sine stupore animi non queo dicere, quod amico nostro, discipulo tuo, sese uolenti exagitare flagitantique insolenter, ut diceret, quid secum ipse tacitus uolueret, Uergilii uersum eum cogitare respondit. cum ille obstupefactus negare non posset, perrexit quaerere, quisnam uersus esset; nec Albicerius, qui grammatici scholam uix transiens uidisset aliquando, uersum ipsum securus et garrulus canere dubitauit.
passages.english: And he at once declared not only the kind of business but also—at which the other cried out loudly in amazement—the very name of the estate, though it was so outlandish that Flaccianus himself could scarcely remember it. Now this I cannot tell without astonishment: when our friend, your pupil, wishing to test him and insolently demanding that he say what he himself was silently turning over in his mind, he answered that he was thinking of a line of Virgil. When the other, dumbfounded, could not deny it, he went on to ask which line it was; and Albicerius, who had scarcely ever glimpsed a grammarian's school even in passing, did not hesitate to chant the line itself, confidently and glibly.

passages.original: quasi aliud ingressus exordium: Morem, inquam, uobis geram et, quamuis post illum laborem scholae rhetoricae in hac me leui armatura nonnihil requieturum esse praesumseram, ut interrogando ista potius agerem quam dicendo, tamen quia et paucissimi sumus, ut clamare mihi contra ualetudinem meam non sit necesse, et istum stilum causa eiusdem salutis quasi aurigam moderatoremque sermonis mei esse uolui, ne concitatius rapiar animo, quam cura corporis poscit, perpetua. ut uultis, oratione audite quid sentiam. sed primo illud uideamus quale sit, unde amatores Academicorum gloriari nimium solent. nam est in libris Ciceronis, quos in huius causae patrocinium scripsit, locus quidam, ut mihi uidetur, mira urbanitate conditus, ut nonnullis autem, etiam firmitate roboratus. difficile est prorsus, ut quemquam non moueat quod ibi dictum est. Academico sapienti ab omnibus ceterarum sectarum m, qui sibi sapientes uidentur, secundas partes dari, cum primas -sibi quemque uindicare necesse sit.
passages.english: As if making another beginning, I said: "I will humour you, and although I had presumed that after that labour of the school of rhetoric I would get some rest in this light armour, so as to handle these matters by questioning rather than by speaking, nevertheless, since we are very few, so that I need not shout against my health, and since I have wanted this pen, for the sake of that same health, to be as it were the charioteer and governor of my speech, lest I be carried away by my mind more vehemently than care of the body requires, hear, as you wish, what I think in continuous discourse. But first let us consider what sort of thing it is over which the admirers of the Academics are accustomed to boast excessively. For there is in the books of Cicero which he wrote in defence of this cause a certain passage, seasoned, as it seems to me, with wonderful wit, but, as it seems to some, also strengthened by solidity. It is indeed hard for anyone not to be moved by what is said there: that the second place is given to the Academic wise man by all those of the other sects who think themselves wise, since each must necessarily claim the first place for himself.
passages.notes: A stray 'm' after 'sectarum' (likely a footnote mark) has been omitted.

passages.original: Nihil ais in philosophia posse percipi et, ut orationem tuam large lateque diffundas, arripis rixas dissensionesque philosophorum et eas tibi contra illos arma ministrare arbitraris. quomodo enim inter Democritum et superiores physicos de uno mundo et innumerabilibus litem diiudicabimus, cum inter ipsum heredemque eius Epicurum concordia manere nequiuerit? nam iste luxuriosus cum atomos quasi ancillulas suas, id est corpuscula, quae in tenebris laetus amplectitur, non tenere uiam suam sed in alienos limites passim sponte declinare permittit, totum patrimonium etiam per iurgia dissipauit.
passages.english: You say that nothing can be grasped in philosophy, and, to spread your speech far and wide, you seize on the quarrels and disagreements of philosophers and think they supply you with weapons against them. For how shall we decide the dispute between Democritus and the earlier physicists about one world or innumerable worlds, when not even between him and his heir Epicurus could harmony endure? For that voluptuary, when he lets the atoms—his little handmaids, as it were, that is, the tiny bodies he gladly embraces in the dark—not keep their course but swerve of their own accord here and there into others' bounds, squandered his whole inheritance, even through lawsuits.

passages.original: si dicis eum nescire quod habeat, redis ad illud absurdum, sapientem nescire sapientiam. si sapientem ipsum negas posse inueniri, non iam cum Academicis sed tecum, quisquis hoc sentis, sermone alio disseremus. illi enim cum haec disputant, de sapiente profecto disputant. clamat Cicero se ipsum magnum esse opinatorem, sed de sapiente se quaerere. quod si adhuc uos, adulescentes, ignotum habetis, certe in Hortensio legistis: si igitur nec certi est quidquam nec opinari sapientis est, nihil umquam sapiens approbabit.
passages.english: If you say that he does not know what he has, you return to that absurdity, that the wise man does not know wisdom. If you deny that a wise man himself can be found, we will discuss with you, whoever holds this, not with the Academics, in another conversation. For when they argue these things, they are certainly arguing about the wise man. Cicero proclaims that he himself is a great holder of opinions, but that he is inquiring about the wise man. And if you, young men, do not yet know this, you have surely read it in the Hortensius: 'If, then, nothing is certain, and it is not for the wise man to hold opinions, the wise man will never approve anything.'

passages.original: illud est capitale, illud formidolosum, illud optimo cuique metuendum, quod nefas omne, si haec ratio probabilis erit — cum probabile cuiquam uisum fuerit esse faciendum, tantum nulli quasi uero assentiatur — non solum sine sceleris sed etiam sine erroris uituperatione committat. quid ergo? haec illi non uiderunt? immo sollertissime prudentissimeque uiderunt, nec mihi ullo pacto tantum adrogauerim, ut Marcum Tullium aliqua ex parte sequar industria uigilantia ingenio doctrina; cui tamen asserenti nihil scire posse hominem si hoc solum diceretur: scio ita uideri mihi\', unde id refelleret non haberet.
passages.english: This is the capital matter, this the dreadful thing, this what every good man must fear: that if this reasoning is to be probable—that when something has seemed probable to anyone as something to be done, he need only not assent to it as true—he may commit every crime without reproach not only of wickedness but even of error. What then? Did they not see these things? On the contrary, they saw them most shrewdly and wisely, nor would I in any way arrogate so much to myself as to follow Marcus Tullius in any respect in diligence, vigilance, talent or learning; yet if, when he asserted that man can know nothing, only this were said to him, 'I know that it seems so to me,' he would have nothing with which to refute it.

passages.original: Hoc mihi de Academicis interim probabiliter, ut potui, persuasi. quod si falsum est, nihil ad me, cui satis est iam non arbitrari non posse ab homine inueniri ueritatem. quisquis autem putat hoc sensisse Academicos, ipsum Ciceronem audiat. ait enim illis morem fuisse occultandi sententiam suam nec eam cuiquam, nisi qui secum ad senectutem usque uixissent, aperire consuesse. quae sit autem ista, deus uiderit; eam tamen arbitror Platonis fuisse. sed ut breuiter accipiatis omne propositum meum, quoquo modo se habeat humana sapientia, eam me uideo nondum percepisse. sed cum tricensimum et tertium aetatis annum agam, non me arbitror desperare debere eam me quandoque adepturum.
passages.english: This much I have meanwhile persuaded myself, probably, as best I could, about the Academics. If it is false, it does not concern me, for whom it is now enough no longer to think that truth cannot be found by man. But whoever thinks the Academics held this, let him hear Cicero himself. For he says it was their custom to conceal their opinion and not to reveal it to anyone except those who had lived with them right up to old age. What that opinion is, God knows; yet I think it was Plato's. But that you may grasp my whole purpose briefly: however human wisdom stands, I see that I have not yet grasped it. But since I am in my thirty-third year, I do not think I ought to despair of attaining it some day.

passages.original: \'iturus\' autem quam \'rediturus\' dixissem securius propter eos, qui putant animos humanos pro meritis peccatorum suorum de caelo lapsos seu deiectos in corpora ista detrudi. sed ego propterea non dubitaui dicere, quia ita dixi \'incaelum\', tamquam dicerem \'addeum\', qui eius est auctor et conditor, sicut beatus Cyprianus non cunctatus est dicere: nam cum corpus e terra, spiritum possideamus e caelo, ipsi terra et caelum sumus. et in libro Ecclesiastae scriptum est: spiritus reuertatur ad deum, qui dedit illum m. quod utique sic intellegendum est, ut non resistatur apostolo dicenti nondum natos nihil egisse boniaut mali. sine controuersia ergo quaedam originalis regio beatitudinis animi deus ipse est, qui cum non quidem de se ipso genuit, sed de nulla re alia condidit, sicut condidit corpus e terra.
passages.english: But I would have said 'going' more safely than 'returning', because of those who think that human souls, for the deserts of their sins, having fallen or been cast down from heaven, are thrust into these bodies. But I did not hesitate to say it because I said 'to heaven' as if I were saying 'to God', who is its author and maker, just as blessed Cyprian did not hesitate to say: 'For since we possess the body from earth and the spirit from heaven, we ourselves are earth and heaven.' And in the book of Ecclesiastes it is written: 'Let the spirit return to God, who gave it.' This must certainly be understood in such a way as not to contradict the apostle, who says that those not yet born had done nothing good or evil. Without dispute, then, a kind of original region of the soul's happiness is God himself, who, though he did not beget it from himself, created it from nothing else, as he created the body from earth.
passages.notes: A stray 'm' after 'illum' (footnote mark) omitted. The last clause is compressed: the sense seems to be that God made the soul not out of himself, yet not out of any other thing as he made the body from earth.
